text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Representative Gabe Vasquez (NM-02) introduced the Socorro Vet Center Act, which would establish a new vet center in Socorro, NM. The bill would direct the Secretary of the Department of Veteran Affairs to establish a facility in Socorro to provide free, confidential social and psychological support to veterans, service members and their families, following on the work of veterans in the community who have come together to do the job themselves.

Across southern New Mexico, many veterans live in rural communities. In Socorro and surrounding counties, the veteran and military population struggles to access services, or get basic assistance with their benefits because the nearest vet clinic, vet center or VA Medical Center can be hours away. This bill would ensure that veterans and our military community across the middle of New Mexico have another closer location to access their hard earned benefits, creating a hub across Socorro, Sierra, Catron, and Lincoln counties.

“Our veterans make a great sacrifice to protect our way of life – when they return home, they deserve easy access to the care they need,” said Vasquez. “In my district, many veterans return home to rural areas where they would need to drive hours just to access a VA medical center. That’s unacceptable – I’m proud to introduce this bill to build a new facility and ease the burden of those veterans in and around Socorro where there is a gap of VA facilities.”

Rep. Vasquez continues to lead the charge to support and expand benefits for New Mexican veterans and our military servicemembers, including:

Spearheading theTRICARE Travel Improvement Act, which Vasquez led and got passed into law with bipartisan support through the FY26 National Defense Authorization Act. The bill lowers the mileage requirement for TRICARE travel reimbursement from 100 miles to 75 miles — helping military families in rural communities more easily access medical care.

Leadingthe New Mexico Rural Veteran Health Care Access Act, a bill to add Otero and Eddy county to the Veteran Integrated Service Network (VISN) 22, so that New Mexico veterans can more easily access care at other facilities far closer to them.

Introducingthe Veteran Education Assistance Adjustment Act, bipartisan legislation to increase the yearly book and supply stipend for student veterans which hasn’t been updated since 2008. If passed, it would increase the stipend from $1,000 to $1,400 and adjust for inflation.

TheFeed Our Veterans Act, legislation Vasquez introduced and fought for during the most recent Farm Bill markup, to combat food insecurity among veterans and protect them from new burdensome SNAP work requirements introduced under the Republican tax law last summer.

Signed a bipartisan discharge petition to require a House vote on the Major Richard Star Act, legislation that would allow combat-injured veterans to receive both their full military retirement pay and VA disability compensation.

title: Turner Imaging Systems' SMART-C® Earns Defense Health Agency Authority to Operate - BioUtah
description:
Military medical teams can now operate the SMART-C on Military Health System networks and send images to existing PACS and electronic health record workflows.
“Warfighters need imaging that moves with them, and the government deserves trusted technology made in America,” said Mike Orthner, PhD, Vice President of Product at Turner Imaging Systems.
Gen2 will build on that foundation with secure, rugged whole-body imaging for military care—from stateside hospitals to the battlefield.
Civilian hospitals and health systems can deploy the same configuration that passed the government’s review, which can shorten their own cybersecurity evaluations.

text:
October 29, 2026

OREM, UT, UNITED STATES, October 28, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — Turner Imaging Systems today announced that its SMART-C®, a cordless, battery-powered, 16-lb mini C-arm that brings fluoroscopy to the point of care, has received a two-year Authorization to Operate (ATO) after working closely with the U.S. Department of Defense Health Agency (DHA). The ATO confirms that SMART-C meets Department of War cybersecurity requirements under the Risk Management Framework (RMF). The authorization followed a rigorous assessment of SMART-C’s security controls, configuration hardening, and vulnerability scanning. Military medical teams can now operate the SMART-C on Military Health System networks and send images to existing PACS and electronic health record workflows. Additionally, the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs recently approved the SMART-C for use with VistA DICOM and is already in use at VA medical centers across the country.

“Warfighters need imaging that moves with them, and the government deserves trusted technology made in America,” said Mike Orthner, PhD, Vice President of Product at Turner Imaging Systems. “SMART-C’s ATO demonstrates its mission readiness. Gen2 will build on that foundation with secure, rugged whole-body imaging for military care—from stateside hospitals to the battlefield. We’re not simply supplying the military; we’re advancing the future of imaging alongside it.”

SMART-C Secure™: available to every customer

The security-hardened software developed for the ATO will be available to all SMART-C customers on request as SMART-C Secure™. Civilian hospitals and health systems can deploy the same configuration that passed the government’s review, which can shorten their own cybersecurity evaluations.

“Hospital IT security teams are asking about device cybersecurity earlier in every purchase,” said Rob Scorcia, Vice President of Sales and Marketing at Turner Imaging Systems. “With SMART-C Secure, any health system can now run the same software that passed a U.S. government cybersecurity review. That puts Turner ahead of the curve and positions us to scale in both military and civilian markets.”

Turner plans to pursue the same authorization for its ENDURO® DR portable digital X-ray system and continues to work with the U.S. military to bring point-of-care imaging to the clinicians who care for service members and veterans.

title: Tricare Young Adult Premiums Near $900 a Month, Straining Military Families
description:
For military families with young adults between the ages of 21 and 26, a familiar budget line item is about to get significantly more expensive.
The Defense Health Agency has confirmed that beginning January 1, monthly premiums for Tricare Young Adult (TYA) will rise to $893 for TYA Prime and $394 for TYA Select.
Back then, more than 26,900 beneficiaries were enrolled in TYA Prime and over 18,200 in TYA Standard.
Since 2016, TYA Prime premiums have jumped 192% and TYA Select premiums have risen 73%.
Only about 1,287 people are enrolled in TYA Prime, while approximately 27,600 are enrolled in TYA Select.
text:
For military families with young adults between the ages of 21 and 26, a familiar budget line item is about to get significantly more expensive. Health insurance premiums for Tricare Young Adult — the coverage program that bridges the gap for military dependents who age out of standard Tricare — are set to climb again in 2027, putting real financial pressure on households that have already sacrificed so much.

The Defense Health Agency has confirmed that beginning January 1, monthly premiums for Tricare Young Adult (TYA) will rise to $893 for TYA Prime and $394 for TYA Select. The changes, which were first reported by Federal News Network, represent increases of 12.5% and 8.5% respectively over 2026 rates. Full details of broader Tricare changes expected in 2027 have not yet been released, but updates to the agency’s operations manual this month confirmed the new premium figures.

Translated into annual costs, military and retiree families with young adult dependents could be looking at between $4,728 and $10,716 in added healthcare expenses each year — on top of what they already pay. By comparison, active-duty families without older children pay nothing in enrollment fees for Tricare Prime and between $50 and $397 per year for Tricare Select, depending on rank and enlistment date. Retiree families pay between $765 and $1,191 per year in enrollment fees. TYA premiums dwarf those figures, and that gap is widening.

A Decade of Steep Increases

The cost of TYA coverage has grown dramatically over the past ten years. A decade ago, TYA Prime enrollees paid $306 a month in premiums, while those in TYA Standard — now called TYA Select — paid $228. Back then, more than 26,900 beneficiaries were enrolled in TYA Prime and over 18,200 in TYA Standard. Since 2016, TYA Prime premiums have jumped 192% and TYA Select premiums have risen 73%.

Today, the situation is nearly reversed. Only about 1,287 people are enrolled in TYA Prime, while approximately 27,600 are enrolled in TYA Select. That shrinking TYA Prime enrollment is a key driver of its skyrocketing costs. When a small group of people is responsible for bearing the full cost of a program — with no government subsidy to offset it — premiums climb fast.

The Defense Health Agency acknowledged this directly:

“A relatively small pool of insured population, combined with a high number of healthcare encounters, result in higher premium rates, particularly for TYA Prime.”

What the Two Plans Actually Cover

TYA Prime functions more like a traditional HMO. Enrollees are assigned a primary care provider — often at a military hospital or contract clinic — and must get referrals before seeing specialists. It comes with no deductibles or copayments, which makes it more predictable but also more expensive in terms of monthly premiums.

TYA Select, on the other hand, gives patients more flexibility. Enrollees can see any physician, including specialists, without needing a referral, and they receive savings for using in-network providers. The tradeoff is a higher deductible and copayments when care is needed.

Why This Program Exists — And Why It Costs So Much

Tricare Young Adult was created in 2011 to give military dependents a coverage option similar to what the Affordable Care Act extended to civilian families — allowing children to stay on a parent’s health plan until age 26. But there’s a critical difference: under federal law, TYA must fully cover its own costs. There is no government contribution to offset what beneficiaries pay. That structure means premiums go up whenever healthcare use increases or enrollment shrinks, with no safety net to soften the blow for families.

For context, the Kaiser Family Foundation reported that the average annual cost of a U.S. family’s employer-provided health plan was $28,303 in 2026 — costs that are largely absorbed by employers, not employees. Military families using TYA get none of that employer-side support.

Families and Advocates Are Sounding the Alarm

The National Military Family Association, an Alexandria, Virginia-based nonprofit that advocates for service members and their dependents, is pushing for answers and for change. The organization says the Defense Health Agency’s explanations don’t “fully explain the underlying factors driving the increases,” and it is working to understand what specific changes in healthcare use or costs are responsible — and why TYA Prime costs are rising faster than TYA Select.

Eileen Huck, director of government relations for the National Military Family Association, warned that rising premiums are creating a dangerous cycle where young adults simply go without coverage.

“It is a vicious cycle because the costs are fully borne by the beneficiary. There’s no government offset. So, as the costs have gone up, young people who either can find less expensive options or feel that they are healthy enough to go without, risk going without health coverage,”

Huck told Military Times in an interview.

TYA is available to unmarried dependents under age 26 of Tricare-eligible sponsors, but only if those young adults don’t have access to employer-offered health insurance and don’t qualify to remain on regular Tricare. Standard Tricare coverage ends at age 21 — or age 23 for full-time college students. That age cutoff itself is a source of frustration.

“It really makes no sense that health coverage is connected to college enrollment,”

Huck said.

“We’ve always been concerned that large numbers of military-connected young adults are going without health coverage because of the cost.”

Legislative Fix Stalled, But Bipartisan Support Grows

Congress has been working since 2021 on legislation that would let military dependents stay on regular Tricare until age 26 — the same benefit civilian families receive through employer plans. The current version of the bill is sponsored by Rep. Patrick Ryan, D-N.Y., in the House and Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., in the Senate, and has gathered 98 bipartisan co-sponsors.

“We absolutely feel that it’s unfair for military families to have to pay extra for their young adults’ health coverage when … civilian families with employer-based plans get that coverage automatically,”

Huck said.

Short of that legislative fix, the National Military Family Association is pushing for at least one immediate change: allowing all military dependents to remain on Tricare until age 23, regardless of whether they attend college. As Huck put it, a young adult’s access to healthcare shouldn’t hinge on their enrollment status in a university.

text:
FAIRFAX, Va., Oct. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Knowesis Inc. has been awarded a task order from the Defense Health Agency (DHA) to provide Psychological Health Program Management Support Services for the Psychological Health Center of Excellence (PHCoE). The award was made under Knowesis' OMNIBUS IV Indefinite Delivery/Indefinite Quantity (IDIQ) contract, following a competitive best-value evaluation.

The task order runs for a base period from September 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027, with four option periods extending performance through February 2031. Under this task order, Knowesis and our partner ICF Incorporated will deliver technical and operational support across PHCoE's full mission set, spanning business operations, strategic communication and outreach, large dataset management and statistical analysis, psychological health research and research translation, and health promotion and behavior change support for service members and their families.

Knowesis brings a proven record of federal health support services, including prior and ongoing work across the Department of War (DoW) and the Military Health System. The company holds a Top Secret Facility Clearance and ISO 9001:2015 and ISO 27001:2022 certifications, and maintains a Federal wide Assurance through the Department of Health and Human Services to support PHCoE's research, advanced analytics, data management and health promotions requirements.

"This award reflects Knowesis' long-standing commitment to the psychological health and readiness of our service members and their families," said Knowesis Principal, Sheryl Cosing. "Our team will continue our support for PHCoE's mission from day one."

This win builds on our existing portfolio of psychological health operational support and research services across the DoW and the Department of Veteran's Affairs.

Knowesis is a Service Disabled Veteran Owned Small Business and Women-Owned Small Business headquartered in Fairfax, VA, delivering science and medical research; advanced analytics; policy and program evaluation; and technical support services across six federal agencies.
